content: The elbow joint is classified as a ginglymus, or hinge joint, allowing specific types of movement. It is formed by the articulation of three bones: the humerus in the upper arm, and the radius and ulna in the forearm. The olecranon process of the ulna forms the prominent bony tip of the elbow. Movements The elbow joint permits two primary types of movement: 1. Flexion and Extension: These hinge-like movements occur at the articulation between the humerus and the ulna. 2. Pronation and Supination: These involve the rotation of the forearm, occurring at the articulation between the radius and ulna. This movement also involves the wrist joint. In the anatomical position (forearm supine), the radius and ulna are parallel. During pronation, the ulna remains stationary while the radius rotates around it, resulting in the crossing of the two bones in the prone position. The majority of the force transmitted through the elbow joint occurs between the humerus and the ulna, with minimal force being transferred between the humerus and the radius. Conversely, at the wrist joint, most of the force is transmitted between the radius and the carpus, with the ulna playing a minor role. Muscles, Arteries, and Nerves The muscles associated with the elbow joint include: Anteriorly: The brachialis muscle. Posteriorly: The triceps brachii and anconeus muscles. Laterally: The supinator muscle and the common extensor tendon. Medially: The common flexor tendon and the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle. The arterial supply to the elbow joint is derived from an extensive anastomotic network. This network includes branches from the profunda brachii artery, superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries, anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent arteries, interosseous recurrent arteries, and the radial recurrent artery. The nerve supply to the elbow joint is provided by: A branch of the ulnar nerve as it passes between the medial epicondyle and the olecranon. A filament from the musculocutaneous nerve. Two branches from the median nerve. Portions of the Joint The elbow joint consists of three distinct portions, all of which are enclosed within a single synovial membrane. The movements of flexion and extension of the forearm, combined with pronation and supination of the hand, are coordinated at this joint to allow precise hand movements. The hand articulates directly with the distal surface of the radius, while the ulnar notch of the radius moves around the lower end of the ulna. The ulna is excluded from the wrist joint by the presence of an articular disk. Rotation of the radial head around its axis at the humerus enables circular movement of the hand. Ligaments The articular surfaces of the elbow joint are connected by a capsule, which is thickened medially, laterally, and to a lesser extent, anteriorly and posteriorly. These thickened areas are often described as distinct ligaments, including: The ulnar collateral ligament. The radial collateral ligament. The annular ligament. Synovial Membrane The synovial membrane of the elbow joint is extensive. It extends from the margins of the articular surface of the humerus and lines the coronoid, radial, and olecranon fossae. It reflects over the deep surface of the joint capsule and forms a pouch between the radial notch, the deep surface of the annular ligament, and the circumference of the radial head. A crescent-shaped fold of synovial membrane projects into the joint cavity between the radius and ulna, suggesting a division into two compartments: the humeroradial and humeroulnar portions. Three fat pads are located between the capsule and the synovial membrane: 1. The largest fat pad lies over the olecranon fossa and is compressed into the fossa by the triceps brachii during flexion. 2. A second fat pad lies over the coronoid fossa and is compressed by the brachialis during extension. 3. The third fat pad lies over the radial fossa and is also compressed by the brachialis during extension. Terminology: Elbow and Ell The term ell, an obsolete unit of length, is historically related to the elbow. The Germanic origins of the words Elle (ell, referring to the length of an arm from shoulder to fingertips) and Ellbogen (elbow) highlight this connection. The English spelling of elbow may have dropped the second l over time, but a more etymologically accurate spelling would be ellbow for the joint and ellbone for the ulna. Carrying Angle When the arm is fully extended with the palm facing forward or upward, the humerus and forearm bones are not perfectly aligned. Instead, there is a slight deviation, typically 5-10 degrees, in the direction of the thumb. This deviation is known as the carrying angle. The carrying angle is generally more pronounced in females than in males. It can influence how individuals hold objects, as those with a more extreme carrying angle may supinate the forearm to keep the elbow closer to the body. Diagnostic Findings: MRI MRI imaging of the normal elbow includes the following sequences: Coronal MPGR. Coronal IR. Coronal PD. Axial PD. Sagittal PD. Sagittal IR.
